paragraphs.paraphrase: Two travellers (named in the next paragraphs as Telemachus and Nestor's son) arrive at Menelaus's home in Lacedaemon and find him holding a feast for two weddings: his daughter, promised long ago at Troy to Achilles's son, is being sent by chariot to the Myrmidons' city where that son now rules, and his only son Megapenthes is marrying Alector's daughter from Sparta. Megapenthes is Menelaus's son by a slave woman, because the gods gave his wife Helen no more children after their daughter Hermione.

barriers.quote: They reached
barriers.my_reading: Telemachus and Nestor's son, who are only identified in ¶2
barriers.note: The Book opens mid-journey; for two paragraphs I did not know who 'they' were.

barriers.quote: a bride from Sparta
barriers.my_reading: a woman from Sparta; I could not tell whether Sparta is the same place as Lacedaemon, where Menelaus lives, or a different city
barriers.note: Only outside knowledge suggests they are the same region.

barriers.quote: He had given his consent and promised her to him while he was still at Troy
barriers.my_reading: Menelaus had promised his daughter to Achilles's son back during the war at Troy
barriers.note: he / her / him refer to three different people in one clause.

barriers.quote: of a bondwoman
barriers.my_reading: by a slave woman rather than by his wife
barriers.note: archaic

barriers.quote: for heaven granted Helen no more children after she had borne Hermione
barriers.my_reading: Helen is Menelaus's wife and Hermione their daughter, presumably the daughter being married; he had his son by a slave because Helen could have no more children
barriers.note: The text never says directly that Helen is his wife or that the bride is Hermione; the reasoning has to be inferred.

paragraphs.paraphrase: The feast is lively: neighbours and relatives eat and celebrate, a singer plays the lyre and sings, and two acrobats perform in the middle of the crowd whenever he strikes up a tune.

barriers.quote: two tumblers
barriers.my_reading: two acrobats
barriers.note: 'Tumbler' first suggests a drinking glass; 'performing' rescues it.

paragraphs.paraphrase: Telemachus and Nestor's son pull up their horses at Menelaus's gate. Menelaus's servant Eteoneus sees them and hurries in to ask his master whether to unharness the horses of these two noble-looking strangers and take them in, or send them away to find hospitality somewhere else.

barriers.quote: the son of Nestor
barriers.my_reading: Telemachus's travelling companion, later called Pisistratus; Nestor is his father (confirmed in ¶13)
barriers.note: The reader must connect 'son of Nestor' with 'Pisistratus' (¶4, ¶7); who Nestor is only emerges later.

barriers.quote: who look like sons of Zeus
barriers.my_reading: they look noble and godlike, not literally sons of the god
barriers.note: Could be taken literally at first.

barriers.quote: Shall we take their horses out
barriers.my_reading: unharness the horses from the chariot and stable them
barriers.note: Only clear after ¶4 ('took their sweating horses from under the yoke').

paragraphs.paraphrase: Menelaus angrily tells Eteoneus he is talking like a fool: of course he must unharness the horses and bring the strangers in to eat. He reminds him that both of them often depended on other people's hospitality on their long way home, and hopes the gods will now let them stay at home in peace.

barriers.quote: where heaven grant that we may rest in peace from now on
barriers.my_reading: 'where' means here at home: may the gods let us live here undisturbed from now on, with no more wandering
barriers.note: 'Rest in peace' sounds like a funeral wish to a modern ear, and the sentence ending is tangled.

paragraphs.paraphrase: Eteoneus fetches the other servants; they unyoke the sweating horses, tie them at the feeding troughs and feed them oats and barley, prop the chariot against the courtyard wall, and lead the guests inside. The two young men are dazzled by the house, which shines like the sun and moon, and after gazing their fill they go to bathe.

barriers.quote: made them fast to the mangers
barriers.my_reading: tied them up at the feeding troughs
barriers.note: archaic 'made fast'

barriers.quote: they leaned the chariot against the end wall of the courtyard
barriers.my_reading: they tipped the unhitched chariot up and propped it against a wall to store it
barriers.note: Hard to picture leaning a chariot against a wall.

paragraphs.paraphrase: Servants bathe the guests, rub them with oil, and dress them in wool cloaks and shirts, and they sit down next to Menelaus. A maid pours water over their hands from a golden jug into a silver basin and sets a table beside them; a senior servant brings bread and other food from the stores, and the carver brings platters of meat and golden cups.

barriers.quote: When the servants had washed them and anointed them with oil
barriers.my_reading: servants bathed them and rubbed oil on their skin, apparently a normal part of welcoming guests
barriers.note: ¶4 said they 'washed themselves', so who washed whom is unclear; anointing with oil is not explained.

paragraphs.paraphrase: Menelaus tells them to start eating and says he will ask who they are after the meal: they are obviously descended from kings, since poor people do not have sons like them.

barriers.quote: Fall to
barriers.my_reading: start eating, help yourselves
barriers.note: archaic

barriers.quote: for the lineage of such men as you cannot have been lost
barriers.my_reading: your noble ancestry has not faded away: it shows plainly in you
barriers.note: Twisted negative phrasing; I had to read it twice.

paragraphs.paraphrase: Menelaus hands them a choice piece of roast loin from his own portion and they eat. When they have finished, Telemachus whispers to Pisistratus to look at the gleaming bronze, gold, amber, ivory and silver: it is like being in the palace of Zeus himself.

barriers.quote: which had been set near him as a prime part
barriers.my_reading: the best cut, served to Menelaus as the host's portion of honour, which he passes on to his guests

barriers.quote: they laid their hands on the good things that were before them
barriers.my_reading: they started eating the food in front of them
barriers.note: Old formula; recurs in ¶18.

paragraphs.paraphrase: Menelaus overhears and says no mortal can rival Zeus, whose house is everlasting; he may or may not be the richest of men, but he gathered his wealth over nearly eight years of wandering home from Troy, through Cyprus, Phoenicia, Egypt, the Ethiopians, Sidonians, Erembians and Libya with its wonderfully fertile flocks. Meanwhile his brother was treacherously murdered through the brother's own wife, so his riches give him no pleasure; he would gladly have only a third of them if he had stayed home and the men who died at Troy were still alive. He mourns them all, but most of all one man who worked and risked more than any Greek and whose fate is unknown, whose old father, wife Penelope and son Telemachus (left as a baby) are grieving: Odysseus, though Menelaus does not yet know that Telemachus is sitting before him.

barriers.quote: the sheep lamb down three times a year
barriers.my_reading: the ewes give birth to lambs three times a year

barriers.quote: whether master or man
barriers.my_reading: whether owner or servant
barriers.note: 'man' meaning servant is archaic

barriers.quote: my brother was secretly and shockingly murdered through the treachery of his wicked wife
barriers.my_reading: Menelaus's brother (named Agamemnon only in ¶42) was killed through the betrayal of his own wife
barriers.note: Who the brother and wife are is not said here; names from outside knowledge only.

barriers.quote: my heavy loss in the ruin of a stately mansion, fully and magnificently furnished
barriers.my_reading: some rich house was destroyed or plundered, perhaps Menelaus's own house while he was away, perhaps his brother's; the text does not say which

barriers.quote: I wish I had only a third of what I now have, so long as I had stayed at home
barriers.my_reading: I would gladly have a third of my wealth if only I had stayed home (and the dead at Troy were alive)
barriers.note: 'so long as' is used for 'if only'.

barriers.quote: far from Argos
barriers.my_reading: far from home; 'Argos' seems to stand for the Greek homeland in general
barriers.note: Argos, Argives, Achaeans, Lacedaemon and Sparta are never distinguished.

barriers.quote: no one of all the Achaeans
barriers.my_reading: the Greeks, especially the army that fought at Troy
barriers.note: Never explained; used throughout the Book.

barriers.quote: He took nothing by it
barriers.my_reading: he gained nothing from all his efforts
barriers.note: archaic idiom

paragraphs.paraphrase: Hearing his father spoken of, Telemachus weeps and holds his cloak over his face. Menelaus notices and hesitates between letting the young man speak in his own time and asking him outright what is wrong.

Before Menelaus decides, Helen comes down from her fragrant upstairs room, as beautiful as the goddess Artemis, and three women (apparently her maids) bring her a chair, a rug and her silver workbasket. The narrator explains that the basket was a gift from Alcandra, wife of the rich Polybus of Egyptian Thebes, who also gave Menelaus silver baths, tripods and gold. The wheeled basket, full of yarn with a distaff of violet wool on top, is set beside Helen, who sits down and begins questioning her husband.

barriers.quote: Adraste brought her a seat, Alcippe a soft woolen rug, while Phylo fetched her
barriers.my_reading: Adraste, Alcippe and Phylo are Helen's maidservants
barriers.note: Never stated.

barriers.quote: two tripods
barriers.my_reading: three-legged metal cauldrons or stands, valued as rich gifts
barriers.note: A modern reader pictures a camera tripod; why it is a lavish gift is unexplained.

barriers.quote: ten talents of gold
barriers.my_reading: a large weight of gold; a 'talent' seems to be an ancient unit of weight or money
barriers.note: Modern 'talent' means a skill; recurs in ¶43.

barriers.quote: a golden distaff
barriers.my_reading: a rod used for holding wool while spinning thread
barriers.note: Unfamiliar tool; appears twice in the paragraph.

paragraphs.paraphrase: Helen asks Menelaus whether they know who the strangers are, and says she must speak her mind even if she is wrong: she has never seen such a likeness as this young man's to Telemachus, Odysseus's son, who was a baby when the Greeks went to war at Troy because of her.

barriers.quote: Shall I guess right or wrong?—but I cannot help saying what I think
barriers.my_reading: I may be wrong, but I have to say it

barriers.quote: on account of my most shameless self
barriers.my_reading: the war was fought because of her, and she calls herself shameless for it
barriers.note: How she caused the war is not explained; outside knowledge only (her leaving with Paris).

paragraphs.paraphrase: Menelaus agrees the young man looks like Odysseus in his hands, feet, hair, head and eyes, and adds that he wept and hid his face in his cloak when Menelaus spoke of Odysseus's sufferings on Menelaus's behalf.

barriers.quote: how much he had suffered on my account
barriers.my_reading: Odysseus suffered in a war fought for Menelaus, to win back his wife Helen
barriers.note: The connection is only implied.

paragraphs.paraphrase: Pisistratus confirms that the young man is Telemachus, explaining that he is too modest to launch into conversation with someone as impressive as Menelaus, and that Pisistratus's father Nestor sent him as escort because Telemachus wants Menelaus's advice. He adds that a son whose father is away has no one to back him at home, which is Telemachus's situation.

barriers.quote: is ashamed to come here and start a conversation
barriers.my_reading: feels it would be presumptuous, on first arriving, to start talking; he is shy, not guilty
barriers.note: 'Ashamed' now suggests guilt, and 'come here' is odd since he has already arrived.

paragraphs.paraphrase: Menelaus is moved to have the son of his dear friend, who suffered so much for him, as his guest. He says he had planned to honour Odysseus after the war by giving him a city in Argos, moving him with his goods, son and people from Ithaca into one of Menelaus's own subject towns so they could live side by side as friends until death, but the gods begrudged them this and kept Odysseus from ever getting home.

barriers.quote: I should have founded a city for him in Argos
barriers.my_reading: I would have founded a city for him (had he come home), not 'I ought to have'
barriers.note: Older 'should have' = 'would have'; a modern reader may read it as regret for a duty neglected.

barriers.quote: should have sacked for them some one of the neighboring cities that are subject to me
barriers.my_reading: he would have cleared the inhabitants out of one of his own subject towns to give it to Odysseus's people
barriers.note: 'Sack' today means plunder, destroy or fire; it seems strange that he would attack his own subject city.

barriers.quote: in Argos
barriers.my_reading: in Menelaus's own realm, apparently; elsewhere Argos seems to mean Greece in general

paragraphs.paraphrase: Everyone weeps: Helen, Telemachus and Menelaus, and Pisistratus too, remembering his brother Antilochus, who was killed by the son of the Dawn goddess. Then Pisistratus speaks to Menelaus.

barriers.quote: whom the son of bright Dawn had killed
barriers.my_reading: a warrior who was the son of the goddess Dawn (not named) killed Antilochus
barriers.note: Dawn as a person with a son is not explained; outside knowledge only.

paragraphs.paraphrase: Pisistratus, recalling that his father Nestor praised Menelaus's good sense, politely asks him to stop the weeping during supper: there will be time to mourn in the morning, and tears and shaving the head are all anyone can give the dead. He mentions his own brother Antilochus, killed at Troy, a fast runner and brave fighter whom Menelaus must have known but whom Pisistratus never met.

barriers.quote: If, then, it is possible, do as I would urge you
barriers.my_reading: a polite request that they stop weeping now, at supper
barriers.note: The actual request is never stated outright.

barriers.quote: in the hours before noon I do not care how much I cry
barriers.my_reading: I don't mind crying as much as needed in the morning, the proper time for mourning
barriers.note: 'I do not care' first reads as 'I'm indifferent'.

barriers.quote: We can only shave our heads for them and wring the tears from our cheeks
barriers.my_reading: the customary ways of mourning: cutting off one's hair and weeping
barriers.note: Head-shaving as mourning is not explained; 'wring the tears from our cheeks' is hard to picture.

barriers.quote: I never set eyes on him myself
barriers.my_reading: Pisistratus was too young, or not yet born, when his brother left for the war, so he never knew him
barriers.note: Surprising that he never met his own brother; no reason is given.

paragraphs.paraphrase: Menelaus praises Pisistratus as wise beyond his years, like his father Nestor, whom the gods have blessed with a good wife, fine brave sons and a vigorous old age at home. He agrees they should stop weeping and go back to their meal, orders water for their hands, and says he and Telemachus will talk fully in the morning.

barriers.quote: One can soon see when a man is son to one whom heaven has blessed both in his wife and in his children
barriers.my_reading: it is easy to recognise the son of a man whom the gods blessed with a good marriage and family, as you are

barriers.quote: a green old age
barriers.my_reading: a healthy, vigorous old age
barriers.note: This sense of 'green' is unfamiliar.

barriers.quote: Let water be poured over our hands
barriers.my_reading: they wash their hands again before going back to eating, apparently a mealtime ritual
barriers.note: They already washed their hands in ¶5.

paragraphs.paraphrase: A servant named Asphalion pours water over their hands and they go back to eating.

Helen, daughter of Zeus, secretly puts a drug into the wine that takes away all grief and anger, so that whoever drinks it cannot cry for the rest of the day even if his parents die or his brother or son is cut down before his eyes. She got it from Polydamna, wife of Thon, in Egypt, a land rich in both healing and poisonous herbs where everyone is a skilled doctor; after having the wine served round, she begins to speak.

barriers.quote: Zeus’s daughter Helen
barriers.my_reading: Helen is literally a daughter of the god Zeus
barriers.note: Surprising and unexplained; ¶46 later calls Menelaus Zeus's son-in-law.

barriers.quote: some good to put into the mixing-bowl
barriers.my_reading: the bowl in which wine is mixed (with water) before it is served
barriers.note: The custom of mixing wine is not explained.

barriers.quote: of such sovereign power and virtue
barriers.my_reading: supremely effective and potent
barriers.note: archaic senses of 'sovereign' and 'virtue'

barriers.quote: for they are of the race of Paeeon
barriers.my_reading: they are descended from Paeeon, apparently a legendary healer or god of medicine
barriers.note: Paeeon is not explained.

paragraphs.paraphrase: Helen addresses Menelaus and the guests, remarking that Zeus hands out good and bad fortune as he pleases, and offers a fitting story about Odysseus at Troy: he disguised himself as a battered beggar or slave and slipped into the city, where only she recognised him. After she had bathed and clothed him and sworn not to betray him, he told her the Greeks' plans, killed many Trojans and got back to the Greek camp with information. The Trojan women mourned, but she was glad, because she already longed for home and regretted that Aphrodite had taken her away from her country, her daughter and her fine husband.

barriers.quote: (which is as Zeus wills, for he is the giver both of good and evil, and can do what he chooses)
barriers.my_reading: whether one is born to good parents, or meets good or bad fortune, is up to Zeus
barriers.note: The aside does not obviously connect to what comes before or after it.

barriers.quote: a tale in season
barriers.my_reading: a story suited to the occasion

barriers.quote: when he was before Troy
barriers.my_reading: when he was outside Troy, besieging it (a place, not a time)
barriers.note: 'before' first reads as 'earlier than'.

barriers.quote: He covered himself with wounds and bruises
barriers.my_reading: he deliberately injured or marked himself so as to look like a beaten slave

barriers.quote: the Argive camp
barriers.my_reading: the Greek camp; 'Argive' seems to mean the same as 'Achaean'

barriers.quote: the wrong that Aphrodite had done me in taking me over there
barriers.my_reading: the goddess of love made Helen leave her home for Troy
barriers.note: How she came to be in Troy is not explained; outside knowledge only (Paris).

barriers.quote: my girl
barriers.my_reading: her daughter, Hermione
barriers.note: Could be read as a maid or a friend.

paragraphs.paraphrase: Menelaus agrees and adds his own story of Odysseus's endurance inside the wooden horse where the best Greek warriors hid. Helen, with Deiphobus beside her and perhaps urged on by a god who favoured the Trojans, walked round the horse three times, touching it and calling the Greek leaders by name in the voices of their wives; Menelaus and Diomed almost burst out or answered, and Anticlus started to reply, but Odysseus clamped his hands over Anticlus's mouth until Athena led Helen away, and that saved them all.

barriers.quote: within the wooden horse
barriers.my_reading: a huge hollow wooden horse with Greek soldiers hidden inside, used to trick the Trojans
barriers.note: The text assumes the story is known; only partly clear from 'our hiding place'.

barriers.quote: you had Deiphobus with you
barriers.my_reading: a Trojan man who was accompanying Helen
barriers.note: Who Deiphobus is and why he is with her is not said; outside knowledge only.

barriers.quote: mimicked all our wives
barriers.my_reading: she imitated the voices of the Greek leaders' wives to tempt them into answering
barriers.note: 'mimicked' could be read as 'mocked'.

barriers.quote: All that you have been saying, my dear wife, is true
barriers.my_reading: he agrees with her, yet his story shows her nearly exposing the hidden Greeks, which seems to undercut her claim that she was secretly on their side
barriers.note: Unclear whether this is a courteous addition or a pointed rebuke.

paragraphs.paraphrase: Telemachus says it is sad that none of this, not even his father's iron courage, saved him from ruin, and asks Menelaus to let them go to bed.

Helen has the maids make up beds with red rugs, coverlets and wool cloaks in a room at the entrance, and a manservant shows the guests there. Telemachus and Pisistratus sleep in the front part of the house, while Menelaus sleeps in an inner room with Helen.

barriers.quote: the room that was in the gatehouse
barriers.my_reading: a room by the entrance of the house, apparently the same place later called 'the forecourt'
barriers.note: Gatehouse and forecourt: two names for where they sleep.

paragraphs.paraphrase: At dawn Menelaus gets up, dresses, straps on his sandals and sword, and comes out looking like a god; he sits down beside Telemachus and speaks to him.

barriers.quote: When Dawn, the rosy-fingered child of morning, appeared
barriers.my_reading: at sunrise, with pink streaks of light (dawn imagined as a woman with rosy fingers)
barriers.note: Stock phrase; recurs in ¶36 and ¶47.

barriers.quote: his comely feet
barriers.my_reading: his handsome, shapely feet
barriers.note: 'Comely' is archaic, and praising feet sounds odd.

paragraphs.paraphrase: Menelaus asks Telemachus what brought him on this long voyage to Lacedaemon, whether public or private business, and asks for the whole story.

barriers.quote: this long sea voyage to Lacedaemon
barriers.my_reading: Telemachus sailed as far as Pylos and then came overland by chariot
barriers.note: They arrived by chariot, so 'sea voyage' is confusing; the crew left at Pylos is only mentioned in ¶49.

paragraphs.paraphrase: Telemachus says he has come for news of his father: his house is overrun by scoundrels who, on the excuse of courting his mother, are slaughtering his sheep and cattle and wasting his estate. He formally begs Menelaus to tell him plainly, without softening anything out of pity, whatever he saw or heard about his father's death, and to repay any service Odysseus did him at Troy by telling the whole truth.

barriers.quote: on the pretense of paying their addresses to my mother
barriers.my_reading: on the excuse of courting his mother
barriers.note: archaic; the idea of suitors helps

barriers.quote: I come as a suppliant to your knees
barriers.my_reading: he is formally begging, as someone who kneels and clasps another's knees in appeal
barriers.note: The gesture is not explained.

paragraphs.paraphrase: Menelaus is outraged that such cowards want to take over a brave man's marriage. He compares them to a deer that leaves her newborn fawns in a lion's den: when the lion comes back he will kill them, just as Odysseus, if he is still as strong as when he threw the wrestler Philomeleides on Lesbos, would kill the suitors and give them a bitter 'wedding'. He then promises to tell Telemachus honestly everything the old man of the sea told him.

barriers.quote: usurp a brave man’s bed
barriers.my_reading: take over his wife and his place in the household

barriers.quote: A hind
barriers.my_reading: a female deer
barriers.note: Unfamiliar word, and the whole simile depends on it.

barriers.quote: will make short work with the pair of them
barriers.my_reading: the lion will quickly kill the two young (the suitors are the fawns, Odysseus the lion)
barriers.note: Which 'pair' is meant (two fawns, or mother and young) is unclear; mapping the simile onto the suitors takes working out.

barriers.quote: they would have a short shrift and a sorry wedding
barriers.my_reading: they would be killed quickly and mercilessly, and the wedding they hope for would end in misery
barriers.note: dated idioms

barriers.quote: the old man of the sea
barriers.my_reading: a sea god, later named Proteus
barriers.note: Introduced before being explained (¶28, ¶31).

paragraphs.paraphrase: Menelaus begins his story: the gods kept him in Egypt because his sacrifices had not satisfied them. On Pharos, an island a day's sail off Egypt whose harbour ships use to take on water, the gods left him without wind for twenty days, and his men would have starved if the goddess Idothea, daughter of Proteus the old man of the sea, had not taken a liking to him and rescued him.

barriers.quote: when they have taken in water
barriers.my_reading: after they have loaded fresh drinking water
barriers.note: 'Taking in water' today suggests a leaking ship.

barriers.quote: the gods becalmed me
barriers.my_reading: the gods kept him stuck with no wind to sail

barriers.quote: saved me in the person of Idothea
barriers.my_reading: the goddess who saved him was Idothea
barriers.note: roundabout phrasing

paragraphs.paraphrase: One day, while his men were off fishing with hooks around the island to keep from starving, Idothea found Menelaus alone and taunted him: he seemed to enjoy starving, since he sat there day after day making no effort to escape while his men slowly wasted away.

Menelaus answers that, whichever goddess she is, he is not staying by choice but must have offended the gods; since gods know everything, he asks her which god is holding him back and how he can sail home.

Idothea explains that an immortal old man called Proteus lives in the sea nearby: an Egyptian, said to be her father, a servant of the sea god Poseidon who knows the whole sea floor. If Menelaus can trap him and hold on, Proteus will tell him the route home and also what has been happening at his house while he has been away.

barriers.quote: people say he is my father
barriers.my_reading: he is her father; the hedge seems to be just a way of speaking
barriers.note: Odd for her to sound unsure of her own father.

barriers.quote: he is Poseidon’s head man
barriers.my_reading: Poseidon's chief servant or deputy
barriers.note: 'Head man' is an unusual phrase; Poseidon's role as sea god is assumed, not stated.

paragraphs.paraphrase: Menelaus asks her to show him a plan for catching the old god off guard, since a god is not easily caught by a mortal.

Idothea tells him that around midday Proteus rises from the sea, announced by a west wind rippling the water, and sleeps in a large sea cave surrounded by his foul-smelling seals. She will take Menelaus there early next morning to lie in ambush, and tells him to pick the three best men from his fleet; she will explain the old man's tricks.

barriers.quote: Halosydne’s chickens, as they call them
barriers.my_reading: a nickname: the seals are the brood of some sea goddess called Halosydne
barriers.note: Who Halosydne is, and why seals are 'chickens', is unexplained.

paragraphs.paraphrase: She explains that Proteus will first count his seals, reckoning them up on his fingers, and then lie down among them like a shepherd with his flock. Once he is asleep they must seize him and hold on ever tighter while he turns into every kind of animal, and into fire and water, until he returns to his own shape and speaks; then they can let him go and ask which god is angry with Menelaus and how to get home.
Idothea dives back into the sea; Menelaus returns, worried, to his ships pulled up on the beach, and they eat supper and camp on the shore for the night.

At dawn Menelaus takes his three most reliable men along the shore, praying as he goes. Idothea brings up four freshly skinned sealskins from the sea to trick her father, scoops four hollows in the sand, has the men lie in them and covers each with a skin; the stench would have been unbearable, but she puts sweet-smelling ambrosia under their noses to kill the smell.

barriers.quote: Who would go to bed with a sea monster if he could help it?
barriers.my_reading: who would willingly lie down next to a smelly sea creature (a wry joke about the sealskins)
barriers.note: 'Go to bed with' can sound sexual, and calling a seal a 'sea monster' is odd.

barriers.quote: she put some ambrosia under each man’s nostrils
barriers.my_reading: a divinely fragrant substance
barriers.note: The text explains its scent; what ambrosia actually is (food of the gods) is outside knowledge only.

paragraphs.paraphrase: They wait all morning while hundreds of seals come ashore; at noon Proteus arrives, counts his seals, including the disguised men among the first, and lies down to sleep. They rush at him and hold on while he turns into a lion, a dragon, a leopard, a boar, running water and a tree, until he gives up and asks Menelaus which god helped him plot this capture and what he wants.
Menelaus replies that Proteus already knows: he has been stuck on the island a long time and is losing heart, so he asks which god is holding him back and how he can sail home.

Proteus tells him that to get home quickly he must offer sacrifices to Zeus and the other gods before setting sail: it is fated that he will not reach home until he has gone back to the river of Egypt and made great sacrifices there, after which the gods will let him finish his voyage.

barriers.quote: the heaven-fed stream of Egypt
barriers.my_reading: the great river of Egypt (the Nile), fed by rain from the sky
barriers.note: The river is not named; outside knowledge only.

paragraphs.paraphrase: Menelaus is heartbroken at having to sail all the way back to Egypt but agrees to do it. He then asks Proteus whether all the Greeks whom he and Nestor left behind at Troy got home safely, or whether any died at sea or among their own people after the war.

barriers.quote: all that long and terrible voyage to Egypt
barriers.my_reading: going back to the river of Egypt feels to him like a long, dreadful journey
barriers.note: ¶28 said Pharos is only a day's sail from Egypt, so why the trip is 'long and terrible' is unclear.

paragraphs.paraphrase: Proteus warns Menelaus that the news will make him weep: many are dead and many alive, but only two leading Greeks died on the way home (Menelaus saw for himself who fell in battle), and a third is alive but stranded at sea. The first is Ajax: Poseidon wrecked him on the rocks of Gyrae but let him reach safety, and he would have survived despite Athena's hatred if he had not boasted that the gods could not drown him; Poseidon then split the rock with his trident, and Ajax fell into the sea with it and drowned.

barriers.quote: only two of the chief men among the Achaeans perished during their return home
barriers.my_reading: Ajax and Menelaus's brother Agamemnon, as the story goes on to tell
barriers.note: The two are only identified over the following paragraphs.

barriers.quote: in spite of all Athena’s hatred
barriers.my_reading: Athena hated Ajax for some reason not given
barriers.note: Why is not explained; outside knowledge only.

paragraphs.paraphrase: Proteus goes on: Menelaus's brother Agamemnon escaped with his ships under the goddess Hera's protection, but near Cape Malea a gale blew him out to sea toward the headland where Thyestes once lived and Aegisthus now lived. Then the gods turned the wind back, they reached home, and Agamemnon kissed the ground and wept for joy.

barriers.quote: the high promontory of Malea
barriers.my_reading: a high headland or cape called Malea

barriers.quote: drove him to the headland where Thyestes used to live, but where Aegisthus was living then
barriers.my_reading: a stretch of coast that had belonged to Thyestes and now belonged to Aegisthus; the storm blew Agamemnon there, and then a change of wind took him home
barriers.note: Who Thyestes and Aegisthus are, how they are related, and how this place relates to Agamemnon's home are not explained; outside knowledge only.

barriers.quote: the gods backed the wind into its old quarter
barriers.my_reading: the gods turned the wind back to its earlier, favourable direction
barriers.note: 'Quarter' as a compass direction is unfamiliar.

paragraphs.paraphrase: Aegisthus had paid a watchman two talents of gold to keep lookout for a whole year so that Agamemnon could not arrive unnoticed and gather his forces. When the watchman reported Agamemnon's arrival, Aegisthus hid twenty warriors on one side of a hall, laid a banquet on the other, invited Agamemnon, and after the meal killed him like an ox in a slaughterhouse; all of Agamemnon's men and all of Aegisthus's men died there in the fighting.

barriers.quote: did not give him the slip and prepare war
barriers.my_reading: so that Agamemnon would not get past the watchman unseen and raise a force to fight Aegisthus
barriers.note: Why Aegisthus feared Agamemnon at all is not explained.

barriers.quote: who at once began to lay a plot for him
barriers.my_reading: Aegisthus is the murderer; presumably he is connected to the 'wicked wife' Menelaus spoke of in ¶8, but the text never links them
barriers.note: The wife's part in the murder is never told; outside knowledge only (Aegisthus is her lover).

barriers.quote: on one side of the gallery
barriers.my_reading: a covered hall or colonnade in Aegisthus's house
barriers.note: 'Gallery' suggests an art gallery or a balcony; recurs in ¶68.

barriers.quote: nor even one of Aegisthus’s
barriers.my_reading: Aegisthus's own men were also killed, presumably fighting Agamemnon's followers
barriers.note: Surprising; who killed them is not said.

paragraphs.paraphrase: Menelaus sank down on the sand weeping, feeling he could not bear to go on living. When he had cried himself out, Proteus told him to stop wasting time on tears and hurry home: Aegisthus might still be alive, or, if Orestes has already killed him, Menelaus might at least arrive in time for the funeral.

barriers.quote: even though Orestes has been beforehand with you in killing him
barriers.my_reading: Orestes may already have killed Aegisthus before Menelaus could; Orestes is presumably Agamemnon's avenger (outside knowledge: his son)
barriers.note: 'Been beforehand with you' is archaic, and Orestes is not identified.

barriers.quote: you may yet come in for his funeral
barriers.my_reading: Menelaus might still arrive in time for Aegisthus's funeral
barriers.note: 'His' could be read as Agamemnon's funeral; 'come in for' is dated.

paragraphs.paraphrase: Menelaus, somewhat comforted, says he now knows about those two and asks about the third man Proteus mentioned: is he alive but stuck at sea, or dead? He wants to know however much it hurts.

barriers.quote: At this I took comfort
barriers.my_reading: the prospect of getting home in time to see Aegisthus punished consoles him
barriers.note: Why this is comforting is not spelled out.

barriers.quote: I know, then, about these two
barriers.my_reading: Ajax and Agamemnon, the two leaders who died on the way home
barriers.note: The last two names mentioned were Aegisthus and Orestes, so 'these two' can be attached to the wrong people.

paragraphs.paraphrase: Proteus says the third man is Odysseus, whom he can see weeping on an island where the nymph Calypso holds him captive with no ship or crew. As for Menelaus, he will not die in Argos: the gods will take him to the Elysian plain at the end of the world, ruled by Rhadamanthus, where there is no rain, hail or snow and a refreshing west wind blows from the ocean, because as Helen's husband he is Zeus's son-in-law.

barriers.quote: you shall not die in Argos, but the gods will take you to the Elysian plain
barriers.my_reading: he will be taken alive to a paradise instead of dying
barriers.note: Unclear whether he dies somewhere else or never dies.

barriers.quote: Oceanus breathes ever with a West wind
barriers.my_reading: the great Ocean, pictured as a god, constantly sends a gentle west wind
barriers.note: Oceanus is not explained.

paragraphs.paraphrase: Proteus dives away; Menelaus goes back to the ships with his men, worried, and they camp for the night. At dawn they launch and row out, he returns to the river of Egypt and makes the required sacrifices, builds a memorial mound for Agamemnon, and then sails home quickly on a fair wind.

barriers.quote: put our masts and sails within them
barriers.my_reading: set up the masts and loaded the sails aboard (they had been taken down while the ships were beached)
barriers.note: Hard to picture masts 'within' ships; recurs in ¶71.

barriers.quote: I raised a mound to the memory of Agamemnon
barriers.my_reading: he built an earth mound as a memorial tomb (without the body)

paragraphs.paraphrase: Menelaus invites Telemachus to stay ten or twelve more days and then promises to send him off with gifts: a chariot and three horses, and a beautiful cup so that he will remember Menelaus every time he pours an offering to the gods.

barriers.quote: whenever you make a drink offering to the immortal gods
barriers.my_reading: whenever he pours out wine as an offering to the gods
barriers.note: The ritual is not explained.

paragraphs.paraphrase: Telemachus politely declines to stay: he could happily listen to Menelaus for a year, but his crew waiting at Pylos is impatient. He asks for a precious object instead of horses, because rocky Ithaca, fit for goats, has no flat ground or racecourses, unlike Menelaus's rich plains of grain and fodder, and he loves his island all the more for it.

barriers.quote: a piece of plate
barriers.my_reading: a valuable vessel of silver or gold (like the mixing-bowl in ¶50), not a dinner plate
barriers.note: Most readers would picture a dinner plate.

barriers.quote: where lotus thrives
barriers.my_reading: some fodder plant growing in the fields, not the water flower

paragraphs.paraphrase: Menelaus smiles, takes his hand, and says his answer shows good breeding; he will swap the horses for the finest treasure in his house: a silver mixing-bowl with a gold rim, made by Hephaestus himself and given to Menelaus by Phaedimus, king of the Sidonians, when he stayed there on his way home.

barriers.quote: a mixing-bowl by Hephaestus’s own hand
barriers.my_reading: made by Hephaestus, apparently a craftsman god, so a priceless object
barriers.note: Hephaestus is not explained; outside knowledge only (smith god).

paragraphs.paraphrase: While they talk, guests keep arriving at Menelaus's house bringing sheep and wine, with bread their wives packed for them, and they cook their meals in the courtyards.

barriers.quote: guests kept coming to the king’s house
barriers.my_reading: people arriving for a feast, perhaps the wedding celebration from ¶0
barriers.note: Who they are and why they bring their own food is unexplained, and the scene then breaks off abruptly.

barriers.quote: their wives had put up bread for them
barriers.my_reading: their wives had packed bread for them to bring
barriers.note: dated sense of 'put up'

paragraphs.paraphrase: Meanwhile, back in Ithaca, the suitors are amusing themselves throwing discuses and javelins in front of Odysseus's house, as insolent as ever. Their leaders, Antinous and Eurymachus, are sitting together when Noemon, son of Phronius, comes up to Antinous.

barriers.quote: Meanwhile the suitors
barriers.my_reading: the scene switches to Ithaca, Telemachus's home, and the men courting his mother
barriers.note: Abrupt change of place with no transition.

paragraphs.paraphrase: Noemon asks Antinous when Telemachus is due back from Pylos, because Telemachus has Noemon's ship and Noemon needs it to go to Elis, where he keeps twelve breeding mares with young, untrained mules, one of which he wants to bring back and train.

barriers.quote: twelve brood mares there with yearling mule foals by their side not yet broken in
barriers.my_reading: twelve breeding mares, each with a year-old mule foal that has not yet been trained
barriers.note: horse-breeding vocabulary

paragraphs.paraphrase: The suitors are stunned: they had been confident Telemachus had not gone to Pylos, thinking he was just out on the farm with the sheep or the swineherd. Antinous questions Noemon: when did he leave, which young men went with him (free citizens or his own servants), and did Noemon lend the ship willingly or was it taken without permission?

barriers.quote: for they had made sure that Telemachus had not gone
barriers.my_reading: they had felt certain (not that they had checked or prevented it)
barriers.note: Modern 'made sure' means ensured or verified; recurs in ¶57.

barriers.quote: the city of Neleus
barriers.my_reading: Pylos, the city Telemachus went to
barriers.note: Neleus is never explained; the link to Pylos has to be inferred from Noemon's question.

barriers.quote: Were they freemen or his own bondservants—for he might manage that too?
barriers.my_reading: did he crew the ship with free men or with his own slaves, since he could have done that as well
barriers.note: The aside 'he might manage that too' is hard to follow.

paragraphs.paraphrase: Noemon says he lent the ship because he could hardly refuse a man of Telemachus's standing in need. The crew were the best young men of the island, and Mentor went aboard as captain, or a god looking exactly like him, which puzzles Noemon because he saw Mentor in Ithaca yesterday morning even though Mentor had supposedly sailed for Pylos.

barriers.quote: I saw Mentor here myself yesterday morning, and yet he was then setting out for Pylos
barriers.my_reading: Noemon saw Mentor board for Pylos days ago, yet saw him here yesterday, so the one who sailed must have been a god in disguise
barriers.note: 'Then' seems to put both events at the same moment, which garbles the contradiction.

paragraphs.paraphrase: Noemon goes home. Antinous and Eurymachus, furious, call the other suitors away from their games to sit with them, and Antinous, son of Eupeithes, speaks in a black rage.

Antinous says Telemachus's voyage is serious: they were sure it would come to nothing, but the young man has slipped away with a hand-picked crew and will cause trouble, and he hopes Zeus destroys him before he grows up. He asks for a ship and twenty men so he can ambush Telemachus in the strait between Ithaca and Samos and make him regret his search for his father.

barriers.quote: may Zeus take him before he is full grown
barriers.my_reading: may Zeus kill him before he becomes a grown man

barriers.quote: we had made sure that it would come to nothing
barriers.my_reading: we had felt certain it would come to nothing
barriers.note: Old sense of 'made sure' = 'felt confident' (see ¶54).

paragraphs.paraphrase: The others approve, and they all go indoors.

The servant Medon overhears the plot from outside the courtyard and goes to tell Penelope. As he enters, she assumes the suitors have sent him to order the maids to cook for them, wishes this could be their very last feast anywhere, and reproaches them for forgetting how kind and fair Odysseus was to their fathers, never high-handed like other kings, which shows their bad hearts and ingratitude.

barriers.quote: for the waste you all make of my son’s estate
barriers.my_reading: she seems to turn from Medon to addressing the suitors directly, as if they were present
barriers.note: Who 'you' is shifts mid-speech; Medon is not a suitor.

paragraphs.paraphrase: Medon says there is worse news: the suitors plan to murder Telemachus on his way back from Pylos and Lacedaemon, where he went for news of his father.

Penelope is struck speechless and her eyes fill; at last she asks why her son left her and sailed off in ships, which carry men over the sea as horses do over land. Does he want to die without leaving an heir to carry on his name?

barriers.quote: ships that make long voyages over the ocean like sea-horses
barriers.my_reading: ships carry men over the sea the way horses carry them over land
barriers.note: 'Sea-horses' first suggests the little fish.

paragraphs.paraphrase: Medon says he does not know whether a god prompted Telemachus or he decided on his own to go and find out whether his father is dead, or alive and on his way home.

Medon goes back downstairs. Penelope, too distraught to sit on any chair, throws herself on the floor of her room weeping, and all the maids, young and old, gather round and weep with her, until she cries out.

barriers.quote: in a transport of sorrow
barriers.my_reading: overwhelmed by grief
barriers.note: archaic sense of 'transport'

paragraphs.paraphrase: Penelope tells the maids the gods have tested her more than any woman: first she lost her brave and famous husband, and now her son has gone to sea without a word to her. She scolds them for not waking her when they knew he was leaving, since she would have stopped him or died, and orders them to send her old gardener Dolius, a wedding gift from her father, to tell Laertes, who might find a way to turn the people against those trying to wipe out his family and Odysseus's.

barriers.quote: over all Hellas and middle Argos
barriers.my_reading: throughout Greece
barriers.note: Neither 'Hellas' nor 'middle Argos' is explained; recurs in ¶75.

barriers.quote: there was not one of you would so much as think of giving me a call out of my bed
barriers.my_reading: not one of you thought to wake me
barriers.note: The missing 'who' makes the sentence stumble, especially aloud.

barriers.quote: or leave me a corpse behind him
barriers.my_reading: he would have had to go over my dead body

barriers.quote: who was given me by my father on my marriage
barriers.my_reading: Dolius is a slave given to Penelope as a wedding gift
barriers.note: A person as a wedding present may startle a modern reader.

barriers.quote: tell everything to Laertes
barriers.my_reading: Laertes appears to be Odysseus's old father
barriers.note: The text never says who Laertes is (only 'his own race and that of Odysseus'); outside knowledge only.

barriers.quote: exterminate his own race
barriers.my_reading: wipe out his family line
barriers.note: 'Race' here means family or lineage, not ethnicity; recurs in ¶19 and ¶65.

paragraphs.paraphrase: The old nurse Eurycleia confesses she knew: she gave Telemachus his bread and wine, but he made her swear not to tell Penelope for ten or twelve days unless she asked, so that she would not spoil her looks with crying. She urges Penelope to wash, change and pray to Athena, who can save him, and not to burden the already troubled Laertes, since she does not believe the gods hate the family so much that no heir will be left to inherit the house and lands.

barriers.quote: aegis-bearing Zeus
barriers.my_reading: Zeus who carries the 'aegis', apparently some shield or emblem of power
barriers.note: 'Aegis' is not explained; recurs in ¶67.

barriers.quote: the race of the son of Arceisius
barriers.my_reading: the family of Laertes, who seems to be the son of Arceisius
barriers.note: The son of Arceisius is not identified.

barriers.quote: there will be a son left to come up after him
barriers.my_reading: some male heir (presumably Telemachus) will survive to carry on the family and inherit
barriers.note: 'Him' could be Laertes or the son of Arceisius, and who the surviving son is is unclear.

barriers.quote: go upstairs with your maids
barriers.my_reading: go up to an upper room to pray
barriers.note: Penelope's room already seems to be upstairs (Medon 'went downstairs'), so the movement is confusing.

paragraphs.paraphrase: Eurycleia's words stop Penelope's weeping; Penelope washes, changes, goes upstairs with her maids, puts crushed barley in a basket as an offering, and begins to pray to Athena.

barriers.quote: put some bruised barley into a basket
barriers.my_reading: crushed barley grain used as a ritual offering with her prayer
barriers.note: Why barley belongs to praying is unexplained; 'bruised' = crushed.

paragraphs.paraphrase: Penelope prays to Athena, reminding her of the fat thigh bones of sheep and cattle Odysseus used to burn as offerings to her, and asks her in return to save her son from the suitors' wickedness.

barriers.quote: burned you fat thigh bones of sheep or heifer
barriers.my_reading: burned animal parts on an altar as sacrifices to Athena
barriers.note: The sacrificial practice is unfamiliar.

paragraphs.paraphrase: Penelope cries aloud and Athena hears her; meanwhile the suitors grow noisy in the hall, and one of them speaks.

barriers.quote: throughout the covered gallery
barriers.my_reading: in a covered hall or colonnade of the house
barriers.note: 'Gallery' again (see ¶43).

paragraphs.paraphrase: A suitor remarks that the queen is getting ready to marry one of them, little knowing that her son is already marked for death.

barriers.quote: The queen is preparing for her marriage
barriers.my_reading: the suitors misread the stir upstairs (washing, changing, crying out) as wedding preparations
barriers.note: Why they think this is not said.

paragraphs.paraphrase: The narrator notes that they did not know what was really going to happen. Antinous warns them to stop talking loudly in case it is overheard inside, and to go quietly and carry out the plan they have agreed on.

barriers.quote: they did not know what was going to happen
barriers.my_reading: a hint that things (Athena's help, or their own downfall) will turn out differently than they expect
barriers.note: Ambiguous: it is not clear what exactly they do not know.

paragraphs.paraphrase: Antinous picks twenty men; they launch the ship, set up the mast and sail, fasten the oars in place with leather straps, spread the white sail, and their servants bring their weapons. They anchor a short way offshore, come back to land, eat, and wait for nightfall.

barriers.quote: they bound the oars to the thole pins with twisted thongs of leather
barriers.my_reading: they tied the oars with leather straps to pegs on the ship's side that hold them while rowing
barriers.note: 'Thole pins' will be unknown to most readers.

barriers.quote: got her mast and sails inside her
barriers.my_reading: set up the mast and brought the sails aboard
barriers.note: Same puzzling picture as ¶47.

barriers.quote: made the ship fast a little way out
barriers.my_reading: anchored or moored the ship a short distance offshore

paragraphs.paraphrase: Penelope lies in her upstairs room unable to eat or drink, wondering whether her son will escape the suitors or be killed. Like a lioness trapped by hunters closing in on every side, she turns things over anxiously until she falls asleep and lies motionless.

barriers.quote: Like a lioness caught in a net with huntsmen hemming her in on every side, she thought and thought
barriers.my_reading: she feels trapped and desperate like a cornered lioness, her mind racing for a way out
barriers.note: Hard to picture a lioness 'thinking'; the point of comparison has to be worked out.

paragraphs.paraphrase: Athena creates a dream figure that looks like Penelope's sister Iphthime (daughter of Icarius, married to Eumelus of Pherae) and sends it to stop Penelope's weeping. It slips into her room through the hole for the door's pull-strap and hovers over her head to speak.

barriers.quote: by the hole through which the thong went for pulling the door to
barriers.my_reading: a small hole in the door for a leather strap used to pull it shut; the phantom slipped in through it
barriers.note: Unfamiliar door mechanism; hard to picture.

paragraphs.paraphrase: The dream figure tells the sleeping Penelope that the carefree gods do not want her to grieve: her son has done them no wrong, so he will come home.

In her dream Penelope asks her sister why she has come, since she lives far away and rarely visits, and how she can stop grieving when she has lost her famous husband and now her inexperienced son has sailed away. She is even more afraid for him than for her husband, fearing the strangers he is among, the sea, and the many enemies plotting to kill him before he gets home.

barriers.quote: a foolish fellow who has never been used to roughing it
barriers.my_reading: naive and inexperienced rather than stupid
barriers.note: 'Foolish' sounds harsher than she seems to mean.

paragraphs.paraphrase: The figure reassures her: Athena herself, a protector anyone would want at his side, has gone with Telemachus, and it is Athena, pitying Penelope, who sent this message.
Penelope says that if the figure is a god, or was sent by one, it should also tell her about her unhappy husband: is he alive, or dead and in the underworld?
The figure refuses to say for certain whether Odysseus is alive or dead, saying there is no point in idle talk.

barriers.quote: there is no use in idle conversation
barriers.my_reading: it will not speak loosely or give uncertain answers
barriers.note: Abrupt and cryptic; sounds dismissive.

paragraphs.paraphrase: The phantom slips out through the strap hole in the door and vanishes into the air; Penelope wakes refreshed and comforted by the vividness of the dream.

barriers.quote: the thong-hole of the door
barriers.my_reading: the strap hole in the door described in ¶73
barriers.note: Only makes sense if ¶73 was understood.

paragraphs.paraphrase: The suitors board and sail out, intent on murdering Telemachus. Midway between Ithaca and Samos lies the small rocky island of Asteris, with a harbour on each side where a ship can shelter, and there they lie in ambush.

barriers.quote: Here, then, the Achaeans placed themselves in ambush
barriers.my_reading: the suitors ('Achaeans' = Greeks in general)
barriers.note: Elsewhere 'Achaeans' meant the Greek army at Troy, so this can read as a new group arriving.

book_level: The word 'Greek' never appears: the reader has to work out that Achaeans, Argives and sometimes Argos and Hellas all mean the Greeks and their land. At the end 'the Achaeans' even names the suitors (¶80), and Lacedaemon vs Sparta (¶0) is never explained.

Much of the backstory is assumed, not told: the brother's 'wicked wife' (¶8) is never connected to Aegisthus (¶42–43). Orestes, Thyestes, Deiphobus, the son of Dawn, Paeeon, Hephaestus, the aegis, Laertes (only inferably Odysseus's father) and the son of Arceisius are all left for outside knowledge.

Victorian or archaic wording trips a modern reader: 'Fall to', 'made fast', 'made sure' (= felt certain, ¶54/¶57), 'a piece of plate', 'paying their addresses', 'put up bread', 'lamb down', 'master or man', 'short shrift', 'should have' (= would have) and 'sacked' (¶14), 'a transport of sorrow', 'rest in peace' (¶3).

Rituals and objects appear without explanation: anointing with oil, repeated hand-washing, the mixing-bowl, tripods, talents, the distaff, clasping knees as a suppliant, head-shaving for mourning, burned thigh bones, bruised barley, drink offerings, thole pins, masts put 'inside' ships and the door 'thong-hole'.

Menelaus's long story (¶27–¶47) nests speeches three deep, with Menelaus quoting Idothea and Proteus in single quotes inside double quotes. On a phone, or heard aloud, it is hard to track who is speaking and where each speech ends.

Travel and geography are hard to follow. Telemachus's 'sea voyage' (¶25) doesn't fit his arrival by chariot (the crew at Pylos is mentioned only in ¶49). Pharos is a day's sail from Egypt, yet the return is 'long and terrible' (¶40). Agamemnon's route is unclear: a storm takes him to Aegisthus's headland, then home, then the watchman sees him 'go by'.

Several speeches rely on logic the reader must supply. Menelaus's horse story seems to contradict Helen's claim of loyalty (¶20–21). Penelope turns from Medon to the absent suitors mid-speech (¶59). Noemon's Mentor puzzle is garbled by 'then' (¶55), and Proteus's 'these two' and 'his funeral' have unclear referents (¶44–45).

Stock formulas repeat and feel old-fashioned, though they are mostly clear: 'laid their hands on the good things that were before them', 'When Dawn, the rosy-fingered child of morning, appeared', 'thought of another matter', 'my heart was clouded with care'.
